analysis.one_liner: Barred landlords from filing evictions nationwide during the COVID-19 emergency, plus six months after it ends.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was introduced with 50 cosponsors, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and died there when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have prohibited any landlord from going to court to evict a tenant from a rental home, regardless of the reason, from the day it became law until six months after the government's COVID-19 emergency declaration ended. The only exception was for tenants who committed serious criminal acts threatening the safety of other tenants or staff. It also required landlords to give tenants at least 30 days' notice before requiring them to move out after the freeze ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Renters who lost income because of the pandemic and could not pay rent. The bill's own findings note that 20.8 million renter households already spent more than 30% of income on housing, and that evictions during the pandemic would increase homelessness and work against public health goals. Tenants would keep their homes without accruing court judgments during the freeze.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Renters at risk of pandemic eviction

how_it_helps.text: The bill bars a landlord from filing any court action to recover possession of a rental dwelling, regardless of cause, from enactment until six months after FEMA ends the March 13, 2020 emergency declaration [S3].

The bill's congressional findings state that 36% of U.S. households (over 43 million) are renters, renters paid $512 billion in rent in 2019, and 20.8 million renter households spent over 30% of income on housing in 2018 [S3].
The findings state that evictions in the pandemic environment would increase homelessness and housing instability, working against the public health goal of keeping people in their homes [S3].
After the moratorium ends, the bill requires landlords to give tenants at least 30 days' notice to vacate before requiring them to leave [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Landlords and rental property owners, who would be unable to remove nonpaying tenants through court for the duration and would collect no rent in the meantime; the bill provides no government fund to cover landlords' missed rent, so unpaid rent would accumulate as debt owed by tenants once the freeze ends.

drawbacks.text: The moratorium bans eviction filings but provides no rent relief or landlord compensation, so tenants' unpaid rent would build up as debt they could face after the freeze ends [S3].

The exception applies only to tenants who commit 'serious criminal acts' threatening the health, life, or safety of other tenants or staff, a standard that could be argued over in individual cases while courts are closed to most filings [S3].
The end date is tied to FEMA's termination of the presidential emergency declaration plus six months, meaning the duration depends on a future administrative decision rather than a fixed date [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a pandemic, keeping people housed is a genuine public health measure, and the bill's findings tie eviction directly to homelessness. But the design is one-sided: it stops evictions without funding the rent that stops being paid, so landlords absorb losses and tenants may still end up owing months of back rent the moment the freeze lifts. A moratorium paired with rental assistance would have spread the cost more fairly.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Judiciary Committee on the day it was filed, and the committee never acted on it, so it never reached the House floor before the Congress ended [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Rep. Jesus 'Chuy' Garcia introduced the Rental Eviction Moratorium Act of 2020 on March 23, 2020, weeks into the COVID-19 pandemic [S1][S5].
The bill attracted 50 cosponsors, all House Democrats [S4].
The full action history shows only three entries: introduction, sponsor remarks in the Congressional Record, and referral to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
The bill received no further action and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Landlords and property owners, who kept the unrestricted ability to file evictions under state law throughout the pandemic; renters gained nothing from this bill, though separate relief measures were enacted during the period.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Landlords, who kept full eviction rights

for.name: Jesus 'Chuy' Garcia
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks in the Congressional Record

against.name: House Committee on the Judiciary
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or report after referral on March 23, 2020

sides.party_line_note: All 51 supporters (the sponsor and 50 cosponsors) were House Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill never reached a roll call [S4].

industries.industry: Residential landlords and rental property owners
industries.note: The bill would have barred them from filing evictions without cause for the emergency period plus six months, leaving unpaid rent uncompensated. Their interest in preserving immediate court eviction ran directly against renters' need to stay housed during the pandemic [S3].

industries.industry: Multifamily real estate investors and lenders
industries.note: A nationwide freeze on eviction filings would have disrupted rent collections backing mortgages on rental properties, though it was temporary. The bill died, so no effect actually occurred [S3].
